client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just can't enjoy it — all I can think about is that she's not there, and it makes me feel this hollow, heavy feeling the whole time. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because she's still gone no matter what I say here.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — what you're describing, that hollow, heavy feeling at gatherings, makes complete sense as a part of grief, and it takes real courage to show up here even when it feels uncertain. You're right that talking won't bring her back, but sometimes these conversations can help us carry the weight a little differently, rather than alone. I'm curious — when you're at those family get-togethers and that feeling washes over you, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind about what it *means* that she's no longer there?

client: I guess the main thought that keeps coming up is that she was kind of the glue, you know? Like, she was the reason everyone actually wanted to be there, and now it just feels like we're all going through the motions without really knowing why. And then I start wondering if maybe the family will just... slowly stop showing up altogether, and that scares me more than I want to admit.
therapist: That fear of the family slowly drifting apart carries a real ache to it — it sounds like losing your grandmother also feels like losing the center of gravity that held everyone together. It's worth gently noticing that this thought, "we'll all just stop showing up," is a prediction about the future, and our minds often treat those fears as facts, especially when we're grieving. What evidence have you seen — even small moments — that the people in your family still want to be connected to each other?

client: I hear what you're saying, but it's hard to think of examples right now because everything still feels so raw. I mean, my cousin did text the group chat after the funeral saying we should get together soon, but I kind of dismissed it as just something people say in the moment. I guess I'm worried that if I let myself believe those small things actually mean something, I'll just end up disappointed when nothing follows through.
therapist: It makes a lot of sense that you're protecting yourself from potential disappointment — when you're already hurting, hoping for something and having it fall through can feel unbearable. But I want to gently reflect something back: you noticed that text, you remembered it, which suggests a part of you *wants* it to mean something, even if another part is bracing for letdown. What do you think it would feel like to hold that small moment as a possibility rather than a certainty either way — not a guarantee, but a genuine sign worth watching?

client: I mean... yeah, I did notice it, and I guess I've been thinking about it more than I'd like to admit. But holding it as "a possibility" sounds nice in theory, and I get what you're saying, but in practice my brain just doesn't work that way — it either grabs onto it and builds this whole story, or I shut it down completely to protect myself. I don't really know how to stay in that middle space without it feeling exhausting or fake.
therapist: What you're describing — that all-or-nothing pull between clinging to hope or shutting it down completely — is actually a really common pattern, and it makes sense your mind developed it as a way to cope with pain. The middle space *is* genuinely hard to hold, and I don't want to minimize that by making it sound like a simple mindset shift. I'm wondering though — when you imagine staying in that uncertain middle, what specifically feels fake about it, is it that it doesn't match how you really feel, or more that it feels like you're setting yourself up to be naive?

client: I think it's more the second one — like, if I let myself stay in that middle space and actually believe things might be okay, I'm just setting myself up to look stupid when it falls apart. There's this voice in my head that says "you already know how this ends, so why pretend otherwise." It feels less like hope and more like just... delaying the inevitable hurt.
therapist: That voice — "you already know how this ends" — is worth paying close attention to, because it's presenting itself as wisdom or self-protection, but it's actually making a very confident claim about the future that it can't truly know. There's a real difference between being realistic and pre-emptively deciding on an outcome to avoid the risk of being hurt, and it sounds like that voice has quietly been making that choice for you. I'm curious — where do you think that voice learned that predicting the worst was safer than staying open?

client: I think it learned that a long time ago, honestly. Growing up, whenever I got excited about something — a friendship, a plan, even just a good day — it felt like something would always come along and knock it down, so eventually it just became easier to knock it down myself first. It's like if I'm the one who ends the hope, at least I'm in control of the disappointment.
therapist: What you just shared is really significant — you essentially learned to become your own disappointment before life could do it to you, and at the time, that probably felt like the only way to stay safe. That's not a flaw in you; it was a smart adaptation to a pattern that kept repeating. I'm gently wondering though — what has that strategy actually cost you over the years, in terms of things you might have closed yourself off from before they had a chance to unfold?

client: That question kind of hit me harder than I expected. I think I've closed myself off from a lot of friendships, maybe even a few relationships, because I assumed they'd fall apart anyway, so why bother investing in them. And honestly, sitting here saying that out loud, I can see how lonely that's made me, but it still feels safer than the alternative.
therapist: The fact that you can see that so clearly right now — the loneliness it's created — even while the protective part still insists it's safer, shows a real kind of courage and self-awareness. It's like you're holding two truths at once: the strategy has kept you from pain, *and* it's also been quietly keeping you from connection and warmth that you clearly deserve. I want to ask you gently — if the cost of "safe" is loneliness, does it still feel like the safer choice, or is it just a more familiar one?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. I think... I've been calling it "safe" for so long that I never really questioned whether it actually was, or if it's just what I know. But familiar and safe aren't the same thing, are they — and that's a little terrifying to sit with.
therapist: That distinction you just made — familiar versus safe — is genuinely one of the most important insights a person can arrive at, and the fact that it feels terrifying tells me you're touching something real and true rather than just an idea. You've carried this pattern for so long that questioning it probably feels a little like pulling on a thread that holds everything together, which is understandably scary. But I want you to notice something: you just sat with an uncomfortable truth instead of shutting it down — so what does it mean about you that you were able to do that just now?

client: I guess it means... I don't know, maybe that I'm not completely closed off? But honestly, my first instinct is to dismiss it and say "well, anyone could do that," like it's not actually a big deal that I sat with it. It's hard to let it mean something good about me without immediately finding a reason to take it back.
therapist: What you just did there is so worth naming — you caught yourself in the act of minimizing, in real time, which is actually a remarkable thing to notice. That instinct to immediately take back anything good about yourself is the same protective voice we've been talking about, just turned inward, making sure you don't get too hopeful even about *yourself*. What do you think it would feel like to just let that small moment of openness count, without needing to earn it or defend it?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to just accept it, but there's this immediate pull to say "yeah, but it's not that big a deal." Like, letting it count feels almost dangerous somehow, like if I acknowledge something good about myself, I'm setting myself up to be proven wrong later. I guess that's exactly what you're pointing at, but knowing that doesn't make it feel any less risky.
therapist: You're absolutely right that understanding the pattern doesn't automatically dissolve the risk it feels like — insight and felt safety are two different things, and it's okay that they're not moving at the same speed for you. But I want to sit with something you said: "letting it count feels dangerous" — which means some part of you is already sensing that it *could* count, that there's something real there worth protecting yourself from. What might it look like to take just the tiniest step toward letting it count — not fully, not all at once, but just enough to see what actually happens?
